title: Are We Closing the Right Schools?
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman examines Tulsa Public Schools' plan to close or consolidate 17 schools and asks whether the right schools are closing and whether displaced students will land in better ones. He reviews research showing closures help students only when they move to substantially higher-performing schools. Using 2024-25 academic growth and chronic absenteeism data, he finds the closure list is not simply the district's weakest schools, with six of 14 closing elementary schools showing higher growth than peers that stay open. Across 30 school-to-school comparisons, only nine improve on both measures while 13 are worse on both. He stops short of second-guessing the district's building-level reasons and notes the expected $11 million in savings. His conclusion is that closures can be justified, but districts must show where students go and what supports follow them, because the goal is to operate better schools rather than fewer.
points: Research on closures suggests displaced students gain only when receiving schools are substantially stronger, so destination quality matters more than the closure itself.
Tulsa's list is not a ranking of its weakest schools, since several closing schools show higher growth than comparable schools that remain open.
In the comparisons, only nine of 30 sending-to-receiving moves improve both growth and chronic absenteeism, while 13 worsen both.
Aldeman uses growth rather than raw achievement, paired with absenteeism as a non-academic proxy, and flags that his color-coded table is descriptive, not a significance test.
The practical ask is transparency: where the $11 million in savings goes, and what tutoring, counseling and transition support follow the students.
quotes: The research on school closures suggests they can benefit students, but only under the right circumstances. Studies from Chicago, Philadelphia, and elsewhere have found that displaced students tend to fare better when they move to substantially higher-performing schools.

But closures can also disrupt learning, and simply moving students from one low-performing school can be detrimental. That means districts need to pay close attention to which schools they close, where students go, and whether the receiving schools are prepared to serve them.

It turns out that many of the schools slated for closure are not necessarily the lowest-performing schools in the district. And, many of the proposed school-to-school moves would send students to schools with lower academic growth and higher chronic absenteeism than the schools they’re leaving.

I focused on academic growth because it captures students’ progress over time rather than their raw achievement levels, and I paired it with chronic absenteeism as a proxy for other non-academic factors.
For example, six of the 14 closing elementary schools had academic growth rates higher than Tulsa’s other elementary schools that will remain open.
From my outside perch, it’s hard to know what other options might be available in Tulsa, but I found that 13 of the 30 comparisons would result in worse outcomes on both measures.

The lesson from Tulsa isn’t that districts should avoid closing schools. Closing schools may be financially necessary, and consolidations can create opportunities to offer students better programs and services. But educational consequences have to be part of the conversation. The goal shouldn’t be simply to operate fewer schools. It should be to operate better ones.
